full_judgment:
6. Both the learned Advocate for the petitioner and the learned Assistant Attorney-General also placed reliance on the decision of Bombay Sweets and Company Ltd vs President, Appeal Tribunal 5 ADC 478 and made submissions in different ways. The learned Assistant Attorney General basing on that decision submits that the interpretation given by the Appellate Division holding section 42(4) of the Act not applicable in a given situation was absolutely correct and applicable in the case before us. The Learned Counsel for the petitioner taking recourse to the same decision submits that on the date of filing of the appeal of the said case the appeal was not in form and as such the counting of limitation was rightly made by the Apex Court after taking into consideration some intervening happenings and by excluding them. But the learned Advocate for the petitioner submits that in the present case since the appeal that was filed on 14-10-2004 was in form, the decision of the Appellate Division was referred to above will not apply. We think that the context of the above decision will be of no avail to the petitioner since his case stands on a different footing. 

 7. The only question left for consideration by this Division is whether in the facts and circumstances of the case in hand the Tribunal was justified in holding that the appeal was disposed of well within the time prescribed under section 42(4) of the act on counting of limitation from the date of acceptance of the appeal for hearing by the Tribunal and not from the date of filing of the same. 

 8. We have heard the learned counsel for the petitioner and the learned Assistant Attorney-General at length and considered their submissions. Mr Mohiuddin the learned counsel for the petitioner in support of his contention placed reliance in the decision of the RM Oil Refinery Ltd vs Appellate Tribunal, Excise and VAT 9 BLC 207. We have categorically perused the judgment by the Appellate Tribunal. As it has been already mentioned that the petitioner before the Tribunal sought relief only on the ground that by operation of section 42(4) of the Act the appeal had been allowed by the Tribunal. The tribunal on the other hand did not accept this point holding that the limitation as prescribed under section 42(4) should be counted from the date of acceptance of the appeal and not from the date of filing of the same. 

 9. Admittedly the appeal was filed on 14-10-2004 and by order No. 2 dated 2-11-2004 the tribunal accepted the appeal for hearing and dismissed the appeal on 24-10-2005 within 12 months as required under law. Mr Mohiuddin submits that the limitation of law should have been counted from the date of filing of the appeal i.e. 14-10-2004 since that is the date when the appeal was accepted for hearing as per section 42(4) of the Act and not from 2-11-2004 when the appeal actually accepted for hearing. Therefore, the appeal should have been allowed by operation of section 42(4) of the Act since from 14-10-2004 Tribunal could not dispose of the appeal within 12 months. This submission is misconceived and not in keeping with the provisions of the Act particularly in respect of the interpretation of the relevant provisions governing the issue. Section 42(1) made provision of filing of the appeal. It says, 

 10. On a close reading of all these provisions indicated above as envisage under sections 42(1), 42(1ka), 42(4) and section 196A(3) together we found that legislature consciously separated the stage of filing of the appeal and the phase of hearing of the same after acceptance that is to say that before acceptance of the appeal for hearing there is a filing (দায়ের) of the same and for the purpose of counting of limitation under section 42(4) it cannot be said that it should be computed from the date of filing (দায়ের) as asserted by the learned advocate for the petitioner. For that reason words and phrases “আপিল গ্রহণের পর হইতে” as they appear in section 42(4) of the Act has been rightly taken by appellate tribunal to be the date from which the limitation will run as contemplated under section 42(4) of the Act. 

 12. Let us now view the issue from another angle. From the decision referred to in 9 BLC 207 by the petitioner dealing with the same issue it has been found from the facts of the case that the tribunal received the appeal for hearing on 30-3-1997 and fixed it for hearing on 26-4-1998 (more than a year) and on 3-5-1998 passed judgment and by that time six months limitation under section 42(4) (as it was during that time) had already been elapsed and hence in that case this Division absolutely on the correct interpretation of law held that the appeal should have been allowed by operation if law under section 42(4) of the Act considering the facts and circumstances of that case. So the facts and circumstances of the said case has no manner of application in the present case and for that reason the same is not applicable in the case in hand. Even in that decision in paragraph 7 it has been clearly mentioned that the appeal was received by the Tribunal for hearing on 30-3-1997 thereby the date of acceptance for hearing of the appeal go paramount consideration for deciding the starting point of limitation. 

 13. In the present case we have found that the appeal was filed on 14-10-2004 and subsequently on 24-10-2004, by order No. 1, the Chairman of the Tribunal sent the same to Tribunal No. 2 who by order No. 2 dated 2-11-2004 i.e. only a few days after filing of the appeal accepted the same for hearing and decision was given by the Tribunal on 24-10-2005 which was done absolutely well within the time as contemplated under section 42(4) of the VAT Act. The Tribunal did not commit any illegality in deciding the appeal or it cannot be said that by operation of section 42(4) in the facts and circumstances of the present case, the appeal deemed to have been allowed by the Tribunal. Certainly under section 42(4) of the Act the limitation shall run from the date of acceptance of the appeal for hearing and not from the date of filing of the same.
